reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Classically a non-contact pivoting or deceleration injury with an audible pop, rapid effusion and a sense of the knee giving way
A rapid (within hours) haemarthrosis after a twisting injury is an ACL rupture until proven otherwise
The Lachman test is the most sensitive examination; the pivot-shift correlates with functional instability
An associated Segond fracture (lateral capsular avulsion) on radiograph is nearly pathognomonic of ACL rupture
Female athletes have a higher incidence, related to neuromuscular and anatomical factors
Management is individualised: reconstruction for young pivoting athletes and instability, with rehabilitation appropriate for lower-demand patients
Associated meniscal, chondral and collateral injuries (the unhappy triad with MCL and medial meniscus) are common
reference.pathophysiology: The ACL restrains anterior tibial translation and rotational load. A valgus, rotational or hyperextension force with the foot planted exceeds ligament tensile strength, tearing it (usually mid-substance). Loss of the ACL produces anterior and rotatory instability, abnormal joint kinematics and increased shear on the menisci and cartilage, predisposing to further meniscal tears and later osteoarthritis.
additionalDifferentials: Tibial eminence avulsion in skeletally immature patients
additionalInvestigations: Lachman, anterior drawer and pivot-shift examination
MRI of the knee to confirm the tear and assess meniscal/chondral injury
Radiographs to detect a Segond fracture or tibial eminence avulsion
Aspiration if characterisation of a tense haemarthrosis is needed
Examination under anaesthesia in equivocal or multiligament cases
redFlags: Multiligament injury or knee dislocation with possible popliteal artery injury
Inability to bear weight with a locked knee suggesting a displaced meniscal fragment
Neurovascular compromise after a high-energy mechanism
reference.prognosis: Reconstruction restores stability and return to pivoting sport in the majority, though re-rupture and graft failure occur, particularly in young athletes returning early; irrespective of treatment there is an increased long-term risk of osteoarthritis.
pitfalls: Dismissing an acute haemarthrosis as a simple sprain and missing the ACL tear
Failing to identify a knee dislocation that has spontaneously reduced with vascular risk
Overlooking associated meniscal or MCL injury
Returning athletes to sport before criteria-based rehabilitation is complete
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
